title: Feign Client Declarative HTTP & Resilience4j Circuit Breakers
prerequisites: Understanding of microservice communication and failure handling

progressiveExplaining.eli5: A call center has a phone line to a partner company. Instead of dialing and re-typing the order every time, the operator uses a pre-printed order form: fill in a few fields, hand it over — the form knows the address and format. The center also has an electrical breaker on the line: if the partner keeps failing, the breaker TRIPS, and for a while every new call is immediately answered with 'line busy — try later' instead of waiting on the dead line. This protects the call center from wasting time on a partner that's down, and it gives the partner time to recover.
progressiveExplaining.junior: OpenFeign makes HTTP clients declarative: @FeignClient(name = "users", url = "${users.url}") interface UserClient { @GetMapping("/users/{id}") User get(@PathVariable Long id); }. Spring creates a proxy implementing the interface that makes the HTTP calls. Resilience4j adds resilience patterns: CircuitBreaker, RateLimiter, Retry, TimeLimiter, Bulkhead. Wire them with annotations or a Registry: @CircuitBreaker(name = "users", fallbackMethod = "getFallback"). A circuit breaker trips after N failures, opens for a wait duration, then half-opens to test recovery.
progressiveExplaining.senior: Architecturally, Feign is a declarative HTTP client built on an interface proxy: Spring Cloud creates a FeignClientFactoryBean that builds a JDK proxy; method calls are mapped to HTTP requests via the annotations (contract), using an encoder/decoder (Jackson) and a client (OkHttp/HttpClient). Resilience4j is a fault-tolerance library using decorators: each pattern wraps the function call with a state machine — the CircuitBreaker tracks failure rate in a sliding window and transitions CLOSED → OPEN → HALF_OPEN → CLOSED. In Spring Cloud, the CircuitBreaker integrates with Feign via a custom Feign circuit breaker, or you wrap the client method with the annotation. Fallbacks return a safe default when the circuit is open or the call fails.
progressiveExplaining.underTheHood: Feign's proxy: MethodMetadata is parsed from the interface annotations; invoking a method creates a RequestTemplate, encodes args, executes via the configured Client (with LoadBalancer if name-based), decodes the response into the return type. Resilience4j's CircuitBreaker: an internal state machine with a ring buffer (sliding window) recording call outcomes; when the failure rate exceeds the threshold (e.g. 50% over 10 calls), it opens; while open, calls fail fast with CallNotPermittedException (invoking the fallback); after waitDuration, it half-opens (allows a few test calls); success closes it, failure reopens. Retry decorates with attempts/backoff; TimeLimiter bounds the call duration; Bulkhead limits concurrent calls. The decorators compose as a chain around the Feign call.

codeComparison.title: Raw RestTemplate calls vs Feign + circuit breaker
codeComparison.summary: Hand-rolled HTTP calls with manual error handling are verbose and have no failure isolation; Feign + Resilience4j makes the client declarative and resilient.

modernOrGood.label: Feign client with circuit breaker

interviewGotchas.question: How does a circuit breaker's state machine work, and what is the half-open state for?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: This tests the fault-tolerance mechanics — interviewers want the CLOSED → OPEN → HALF_OPEN transitions and the sliding-window failure measurement that drives them.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: The circuit breaker is a state machine. CLOSED (normal): calls pass through and outcomes are recorded in a sliding window (e.g. the last 10 calls or 10 seconds); when the failure rate exceeds the threshold (e.g. 50%), it transitions to OPEN. OPEN: calls fail fast (CallNotPermittedException) without hitting the downstream service — protecting it and freeing the caller's resources; this lasts waitDurationInOpenState (e.g. 5s). HALF_OPEN: after the wait, the breaker lets a small number of trial calls through to test whether the downstream has recovered; if they succeed (below the threshold), it returns to CLOSED; if they fail, it reopens. This prevents a broken service from being hammered while still allowing automatic recovery. The fallback method is invoked for the failing calls so the caller gets a graceful response instead of an exception.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: The naive answer is 'a circuit breaker retries failed calls'. It blocks calls when open (fail-fast), it doesn't retry — retry is a separate Resilience4j pattern. Another trap: setting the window too small (e.g. 1 call) makes the breaker trip on a single blip, and too large delays detection. Candidates who describe the three states and the window math show real understanding.

interviewGotchas.question: What is the difference between a Feign client and RestTemplate/WebClient, and when would you choose Feign?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: This probes the client-selection trade-off — interviewers want to know the declarative-proxy model's pros/cons vs the more manual RestTemplate and the reactive WebClient.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: Feign is a declarative, interface-based HTTP client: you define the contract as a Java interface with Spring MVC annotations, and Spring generates a proxy that implements the HTTP calls. It shines for typed, synchronous service-to-service calls in microservices (especially with Spring Cloud: load balancing, circuit breakers, request interceptors). RestTemplate is imperative and manual (build URLs, map responses) — more verbose but more explicit; still fine for simple clients. WebClient is the reactive client (Mono/Flux), non-blocking, for WebFlux or when you need streaming/async; it can also be used in MVC. Choose Feign for declarative typed contracts with Spring Cloud integration; WebClient for reactive/streaming; RestTemplate for legacy/simple blocking needs. Feign's proxy adds abstraction that can obscure the actual HTTP call, so debugging may require enabling Feign logging.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: The naive answer is 'Feign is just a wrapper around RestTemplate'. It's a distinct code-generated proxy model. Another trap: assuming Feign is asynchronous — by default it's synchronous blocking; async requires a CompletableFuture return type or reactive support. Candidates who compare the three clients on the blocking/reactive and declarative axes show real depth.
